title: The Empty Ledger
premise: Retired detective Coral Lockridge, drowning in debt at her failing bookshop, receives a confession letter for a murder committed the day after the victim's funeral — a case she worked and never closed. The letter's author knows details that were never made public, including one only the killer could know, forcing Coral to reopen the investigation while dodging her former department, which wants her gone. As she traces the letter through the victim's tangled family and a missing second ledger, she realizes the confessor is someone close to her who has been living under a borrowed identity since the night of the death. In the end Coral must choose between turning in the person she has come to love again and honoring the duty that once defined her — and she finds a third path: exposing the true instigator of the crime, letting the confessor surrender on their own terms.
about_author: Elodie Montrose is the pen name of a former small-town newspaper reporter who spent a decade covering crime courts before turning to fiction. She writes mysteries about memory, guilt, and the quiet violence of ordinary lives from a coastal cottage full of secondhand books.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Coral Lockridge, POV. Three months into retirement, Coral opens shop mail to find a handwritten confession to the murder of Vivian Ashe — postmarked the day after Vivian's funeral. The letter names Coral by an old case nickname no one outside the file ever used. Beat: dread rekindling an old wound.

chapters.title: The Case That Wouldn't Close
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. She digs out her private copies of the unsolved Ashe file and confirms every detail in the letter is accurate — except one: the letter mentions a second ledger never logged as evidence. Beat: the professional thrill of pursuit colliding with fear of what reopening means.

chapters.title: Empty Shelves, Full Ghosts
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Her bookshop faces eviction; her former partner, DI Marcus Hale, warns her off when she quietly asks about the case status. We learn her retirement followed a botched stakeout that broke her confidence. Beat: loneliness and stubborn pride.

chapters.title: The Widow Who Smiled
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. She attends the wake uninvited and observes Vivian's family: grieving husband Daniel, brittle sister-in-law Ruth, and Vivian's estranged daughter Nell, who arrived too late and seems oddly calm. Beat: unease — everyone is performing grief, some badly.

chapters.title: A Ledger in Two Hands
chapters.summary: Nell, POV (first shift). Nell returns to her mother's house and finds her childhood room subtly rearranged, as if someone searched it. She remembers her mother's obsession with a green accounting ledger and hides the memory even from herself. Beat: guilt over years of silence.

chapters.title: Second Postmark
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. A second letter arrives — not a confession but instructions: 'Ask Ruth about the summer house.' Coral realizes the writer is steering her investigation like a hand on her elbow. Beat: the hunter realizing she is also being hunted.

chapters.title: Ruth's Perfect Alibi
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Under pretext of condolence, Coral questions Ruth, whose alibi is airtight and rehearsed. But Ruth flinches at the word 'ledger.' That night Coral's shop is broken into — nothing stolen except her copy of the case file. Beat: escalation; the stakes turn physical.

chapters.title: What Marcus Knew
chapters.summary: Marcus, POV. Hale admits to himself he recognized the first letter's handwriting analysis leak from inside the department and buried it to protect his career. He begins quietly following Coral. Beat: complicity and shame.

chapters.title: The Summer House
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. At the derelict Ashe summer house Coral finds a hidden floor cache: the second ledger, half-burned, recording payments to someone initialled 'T.M.' — and a photograph of a young woman who is not Vivian. Beat: revelation that reframes the whole case.

chapters.title: Daughter of the Ledger
chapters.summary: Nell, POV. Nell confronts her own memories: her mother paid a woman named Tamsin Merrow for years — hush money tied to Nell's real parentage. Nell has been living under a name that was never hers. Beat: identity cracking open.

chapters.title: Two Funerals Deep
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Coral learns Tamsin Merrow died in an apparent accident two weeks after Vivian — unreported, cremated quickly. Two deaths, one postmark window. The confession letter may be for both. Beat: horror at the pattern's scale.

chapters.title: The Man Behind the Counter
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Coral's part-time shop assistant, Theo Marsh, covers for her during a police interview and shows uncanny knowledge of investigative procedure. A dropped receipt places him near the summer house. Beat: suspicion blooming where affection already lives.

chapters.title: Hale's Bargain
chapters.summary: Marcus, POV. Hale offers Coral a deal: her files for his protection from Internal Affairs. She refuses, and he tips off the department anyway, making her a suspect in evidence tampering. Beat: betrayal by the last institution she trusted.

chapters.title: Interrogation by Firelight
chapters.summary: Theo, POV. Theo confronts Coral in the closed shop and confesses partially: he is Tamsin Merrow's brother, living under a changed name, and he sent the letters to force someone competent to look. He swears he didn't kill anyone. Beat: intimacy forged in shared danger.

chapters.title: The Third Letter
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. A third letter arrives, this one threatening Theo by name — meaning the writer isn't Theo and knows he's exposed. Coral sets a trap using the ledger's final page as bait, announcing a meeting at the summer house. Beat: resolve hardening into strategy.

chapters.title: Daniel's Debt
chapters.summary: Nell, POV. Nell discovers her stepfather Daniel mortgaged everything to pay off Vivian's blackmailers — and that Vivian's 'accident' happened hours after he learned Tamsin held the original ledger. Beat: grief curdling into terrible comprehension.

chapters.title: Night at the Summer House
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. The trap springs: Ruth arrives expecting to destroy the ledger, revealing she helped Daniel stage Tamsin's death but believed it was an accident cover-up, not murder. Daniel appears behind her. Beat: terror and pity entangled.

chapters.title: Confession, Interrupted
chapters.summary: Marcus, POV. Hale, tailing Coral, witnesses Daniel confess to striking Tamsin in panic — then realizes Daniel is covering for someone: Nell was there that night. Duty wars with loyalty as sirens approach. Beat: the cost of the badge.

chapters.title: What Nell Carried
chapters.summary: Nell, POV. Nell admits she saw the killing and stayed silent to protect the only parent she had left — and because exposure meant losing her false identity entirely. She wrote the first letter herself, hoping truth could be outsourced. Beat: catharsis through confession.

chapters.title: The Empty Ledger Closes
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Climax: Daniel, cornered, tries to burn the shop with the ledger copies inside; Coral saves Theo and the evidence, choosing love and duty at once. Daniel is arrested; Ruth turns state's witness. Beat: fire, choice, survival.

chapters.title: Names We Keep
chapters.summary: Nell, POV. Weeks later, Nell legally reclaims her mother's name and visits Coral's reopened, barely-solvent shop. She and Coral — bound now by shared truth rather than blood — begin an uneasy friendship. Beat: tenderness after ruin.

chapters.title: First Editions
chapters.summary: Coral, POV. Resolution: Hale retires and leaves Coral the complete case file as amends; Theo stays on at the shop; the final letter, unsigned, simply reads 'Thank you.' Coral shelves a new mystery novel and smiles at the door chime. Beat: peace earned, vigilance kept.
